I will keep my land mainly in the usual wheat-maize rotation. I am in Quzhou County on the North China Plain, so this is the crop pattern I know best, it fits the local weather and water conditions, and it is the safest way for me to get steady grain output. At the start of the growing season, I will continue managing the winter wheat already in the field, then after harvest I will plant summer maize on the same land. I will not spread myself across too many crops, because with my experience and schooling I trust a simple plan I can manage well more than a complicated one I may not control well.

For the winter wheat, I will use an improved variety because I want stable emergence, lodging resistance, and dependable yield. I will fertilize enough to support tillering and grain filling, but I will not push fertilizer too hard because that raises cost and can make the crop too lush. I will irrigate a few key times, especially around jointing and grain filling, because wheat in my area still depends on timely water. I will plough or rotary till where needed to keep the seedbed workable and to manage weeds and residues. I will spray a limited number of times, mainly when disease or aphids are likely, because I want to protect yield without wasting money.

After wheat harvest, I will sow hybrid summer maize right away on the same land. I will do that because maize after wheat is the standard rhythm here and makes full use of the season. I will choose hybrid seed because I want strong vigor and better yield. I will use moderate fertilizer, with more nitrogen than phosphorus and potassium, because maize responds well to nitrogen but I still need balanced nutrition. I will reduce tillage pressure after wheat and move quickly so I do not lose moisture or planting time. I will irrigate when the crop most needs it, especially if summer rain is short, and I will spray mainly for borers, armyworms, and leaf disease if pressure shows up. My whole plan is to stay with the crops I understand, control costs, and aim for a steady harvest rather than gamble on something unfamiliar.
